cells.tense: You are pointing at a direction and letting it be seen where you stand.
cells.ask: Offer one piece of what you carry to somebody who hasn't heard it — a story, a recipe, a way of doing a thing — and let their version differ.
cells.core:
There's a direction you're pointed in, and it isn't private. You pick which of the things handed to you are worth keeping on, and you say so in front of people. Choosing those doesn't mean dropping the rest.

What shows here is the difference between steering something and being steered by it, and you act on that difference. It gets tested in a room where the others already agree with you: the direction can be held there without hardening against the people holding it with you. It doesn't have to turn into the argument. Carry it the way you'd carry something heavy for somebody else — firm, and not squeezing.
cells.sheetLine: You know what you're pointing at, and you point at it out loud.
cells.verb: Choosing which way to point, and pointing
cells.place: In what gets passed between people and kept

cells.tense: You will have rehearsed the direction until nobody could possibly get it wrong.
cells.ask: Say the direction once as a sentence that ends, then leave the room and let it travel without you.
cells.core:
You're bracing for a time when the direction is finally straight with the people around you. So each retelling becomes a chance to make it exact, each hand-off a chance to correct it. What you carry is real. The correcting runs ahead of it.

Nobody receives a tradition the way it was handed over, and that clean future keeps not arriving — which leaves you managing people who aren't in the room. The thing being carried on doesn't need you defending it. It needs you to say it once, plainly, and let the answer be something other than what you said. The direction holds on its own. It doesn't need you standing over it.

cells.tense: You were pointed somewhere and you stopped pointing, and that was a long time ago.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you know and teach it to one person, small and unfinished, before you feel ready.
cells.core:
There's a thing you know that's worth passing on, and you don't pass it. You stay at the edge of the room where this is concerned — near it, not in it — and the offering doesn't come out. What you know is still in you. The pointing stopped.

It might look like keeping your head down, or like not making it about you. Either way, the light you'd go by hasn't gone out; it just isn't being seen. Tending something and letting it grow on its own isn't the same as abandoning it. Care that doesn't clutch. Start smaller than feels adequate, with whoever's nearest, and let it be rough — the size of the offering isn't the point.

cells.tense: The steering is already happening and you keep describing it as just how the work goes.
cells.ask: Say out loud that one thing you keep doing was your choice — the phrase you use, the way you run it — and let it be credited to you.
cells.core:
You're already setting the direction here — in what you pass along, what you let stand, the way a thing gets done now because you do it that way. You'd tell it as the work doing itself, or as how it's been done here. The steering is real. The ownership isn't said.

That's the quieter part: nothing's broken, and nobody's asking you to take a bow. It's that the thing carried forward came out of your hands, and you keep handing the credit to the room. That's not modesty exactly; it's a habit of standing next to your own choices. Holding this without forcing means letting it be known you set it. The direction already runs. Saying so just puts it back in your hands.

attempts.check: The record supports Orientation choosing a direction ('which calling to follow') but never says people will follow it, and never says it has already reached anyone else; I must keep the claim at the person's own steering and dropping, not at its effect on others. A reader could reasonably say that a shared tradition is not mine to steer alone, so the asks are about offering one piece of it rather than redirecting the whole thing. The asks stay useful if my read is wrong because each one is simply a modest handing-over the person can do anyway. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about 'your voice shaping what people carry' — cut.
